office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering the tax structure, natural-resource and timber policy, K-12 policy and funding, and criminal-justice statutes.
race_blurb: First-term Democratic Rep. Adam Bernbaum faces Republican Eric Pratt, a Quilcene field-installation supervisor making his first legislative run. A September forum report described both as wary of raising taxes and wanting local say on road projects; they split most sharply on the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, which Bernbaum voted for and Pratt opposes.

candidates.summary: First-term state representative from Port Angeles and Vice Chair of the House Transportation Committee, a former legislative assistant and policy analyst with a Ph.D. in political science.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 9.9% tax on income over $1 million and defended it as shifting the burden toward high earners [S5][S8]
Prime sponsor of enacted bills on childcare capacity, prescribed-fire insurance and rural middle housing [S11][S13][S14]
Plans a bill to freeze the state energy code for six years, citing housing costs [S5]
Voted for ESHB 1296, which narrowed several parental notification and records rights from Initiative 2081 [S9][S10]
Platform pledges to protect abortion access; endorsed by Planned Parenthood [S1][S3]

taxes.basis: Voted yes on ESSB 6346 and defended it at a forum as shifting the tax burden toward high earners, while saying he won spending limits in exchange.

spending.basis: Points to the budget-spending limits he won and a balanced budget, alongside calls for infrastructure investment and protecting K-12 from cuts.

housing.basis: Sponsored a law easing sewer requirements for rural middle housing, plans an energy-code freeze to cut building costs, and backs permitting reform.

climate.basis: Platform says climate change is real and the region should be part of the solution, endorsed by Washington Conservation Action; tempered by his proposed energy-code freeze.

experience.basis: One-term incumbent and committee vice chair with several enacted bills, running on that record.

local-control.basis: Said communities rather than Olympia should decide on projects like Highway 101 roundabouts; a single forum statement.

healthcare.basis: Focuses on rural hospital funding, affordable insulin and mental-health access within the existing system; no single-payer position.

social.basis: Platform commits to protecting abortion access, contraception and IVF; endorsed by Planned Parenthood.

parental-rights.basis: Recorded yes votes on ESHB 1296, which eliminated or narrowed several Initiative 2081 parental notification, records and opt-out rights and added student privacy priorities.

candidates.summary: Quilcene single father and sports-field installation supervisor, a Precinct Committee Officer who has testified on tax bills in Olympia, making his first run for the Legislature.
highlights: Opposed the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and would oppose all new taxes until the state accounts for current revenue [S6]
Testified in 2024 for Initiative 2111, a ban on state and local income taxes [S5]
Pledges to increase housing supply and oppose regulations that inflate costs [S3]
Says Olympia should not decide local projects such as Highway 101 roundabouts [S6]

taxes.basis: Statement, website, 2024 testimony for an income-tax ban and forum remarks all oppose new taxes, including the 2026 income tax.

spending.basis: Calls the budget 'a little reckless' and an 'ever-increasing spending problem' and wants accounting for current revenue before any new tax.

housing.basis: Pledges to increase housing supply and oppose regulations that inflate costs; opposes over-regulation that impedes housing.

safety.basis: Stands behind law enforcement and supports community policing funding; no specific enforcement proposals.

experience.basis: No office beyond Precinct Committee Officer; presents himself as a citizen 'not as a politician' against a sitting incumbent.

local-control.basis: Says it is not Olympia's role to tell communities what road projects they need and that local voices should shape policy.

healthcare.basis: Would lower drug costs, protect pre-existing-condition coverage and expand rural access, with decisions left to patients and doctors.
